title: Enuma Elish, Tablet III: the assembly of the gods
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.2, Poem of Creation (Enuma elish) (ed. A. C. Heinrich, rev. Z. J. Földi and E. Jiménez), SB III) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Enuma Elish (the Babylonian Poem of Creation), Tablet III: 138 of 138 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (3 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
Anshar sends his vizier Kakka to Lahmu and Lahamu to summon the gods, repeating the account of Tiamat's army and Marduk's demand. The gods gather, feast, and decree Marduk's destiny.

Enuma Elish ('When on high'), the Babylonian Poem of Creation, tells how Marduk, god of Babylon, defeated Tiamat, created the ordered world and became king of the gods. It was written on seven tablets and recited in Babylon during the New Year festival. The date of composition is debated (proposals range from the 18th to the 12th century BCE); the surviving copies date from the 9th to the 2nd century BCE and come from Ashur, Nineveh, Kish, Babylon, Sippar, Uruk and other sites. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/III) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 138 of the 138 lines of the eBL edition (100%), from 3 tablets in the British Museum: K.3473 (Nineveh), BM.42285, K.8575 (Nineveh).
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; (gloss: ...) a note written by the scribe in small signs or in the margin.

translation.text:
1Anshar made ready to speak,
2Saying to Kakka his vizier these words,
3“Kakka, vizier who contents me,
4“Let it be you that I send off toward Lahmu and Lahamu.
5“You know how [to find a way], you can make a fine speech.
6“Send over to my presence the gods my ancestors,
7“Let them bring all the gods before me.
8“Let them converse, sit down at a feast,
9“On produce of the field let them feed, imbibe of the vine.
10“Let them ordain destiny for Marduk, their champion.
11“Be off, Kakka, wait upon them,
12“All that I tell you, repeat to them:
13‘It is Anshar your son who has ordered me to come,
14‘He has bade me speak in full the command of his heart,
15‘To wit: “Tiamat our mother has grown angry with us,
16“She has assembled a host, savage with rage.
17“All the gods rallied around her,
18“Even those you created are going over to her side.
19“They massed around her, drew up at Tiamat's side.
20“Angry, scheming, never lying down night and day,
21“Eager for battle, rumbling, raging,
22“Forming a host, that they might start hostilities.
23“Mother Hubur, who can form everything,
24“Added countless invincible weapons, gave birth to monster serpents,
25“Pointed of fang, with merciless incisors(?),
26“She filled their bodies with venom for blood.
27“Fierce dragons she clad with glories,
28“Causing them to bear glories like gods, (saying)
translation.scan_note: British Museum K.3473: obverse, the tablet's own lines 1 to 28. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/III) attributes SB III 1-28 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges of a tall tablet (about 17 cm) of several joined pieces, ink K.3473 on the right edge and Rm 615 and 79-7-8,296 on the left edge. Both faces are packed with very small script, about 80 or more lines on the obverse and 50 or more on the reverse, consistent with eBL's 85 and 53. On this tablet lines 1-16, 21-28 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken. Lines 17-20 are complete on this tablet.

29‘Whoever sees them shall go numb with terror!
30‘Let their bodies keep leaping forward and never retreat!’
31“She deployed serpents, dragons, and hairy hero-men,
32“Lion monsters, lion men, scorpion men,
33“Mighty demons, fish men, bull men,
34“Bearing unsparing arms, fearless in battle.
35“Her commands were absolute, no one opposed them.
36“Eleven indeed on this wise she created.
37“From among the gods her offspring, who made up her host,
38“She raised up Qingu from among them, it was he she made greatest among them.
39“Leadership of the army, command of the assembly,
40“Arming, contact, advance of the melee,
41“Supreme command in warfare:
42“All she entrusted to him, made him sit on the dais.
43‘I cast your spell, I make you the greatest in the assembly of the gods,
44‘Kingship of all the gods I put in your power.
45‘You are greatest, my husband, you are illustrious,
46‘Your command shall always prevail over all the Anunna-gods.’
47“She gave him the tablet of destinies, had him hold it to his chest, (saying)
48‘As for you, your command will not be changed, your utterance shall endure.’
49When Qingu was the highest, had taken over supremacy,
50He ordained destinies for her divine children,
51‘Whatever you (gods) command shall cause a blaze to die out,
52‘Your concentrated venom shall make the mighty one yield.’
53“I sent Anu, he could not confront her,
54“Nudimmud was afraid and turned back.
55“Marduk came forward, the sage of the gods, your son,

56“He has resolved to go against Tiamat.
57“When he spoke, he said to me,
58‘If indeed I am to champion you,
59‘Subdue Tiamat and save your lives,
60‘'Convene the assembly, nominate me for the ultimate destiny!
61‘Take your places in the Assembly Place of the Gods, all of you, in joyful mood,
62‘When I speak, let me ordain destinies instead of you.
63‘Let nothing that I shall bring about be altered,
64‘Nor what I say be revoked or changed.'
65“Come quickly to me, straightaway ordain him your destinies,
66“Let him go and confront your powerful enemy.”
67Kakka went and made straight his way

Both faces are packed with very small script, about 80 or more lines on the obverse and 50 or more on the reverse, consistent with eBL's 85 and 53. On this tablet lines 86-112 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.

translation.text:
113‘Marduk came forward, the sage of the gods, your son,
114‘He has resolved to go against Tiamat.
115‘When he spoke, he said to me,
116“If indeed I am to champion you,
117“Subdue Tiamat and save your lives,
118“Convene the assembly, nominate me for the ultimate destiny!
119“In the Assembly Place of the Gods take your places, all of you, in joyful mood.
120“When I speak, let me ordain destinies instead of you.
121“Let nothing that I shall bring about be altered,
122“Nor what I say be revoked or changed.”
123‘Come quickly to me, straightaway ordain him your destinies,
124‘Let him go and confront your powerful enemy.’”
125When Lahmu and Lahamu heard, they cried aloud,
126All of the Igigi-gods wailed bitterly,
127“What has gone wrong, that she has taken action against us?
128“We scarcely know what Tiamat might do!”
129They came together in a swarm,
130All the great gods, ordainers of [destinies],
131Came before Anshar, they were full of [joy]
132One kissed the other in the assembly [of the gods],
133They conversed, sat down at a feast,
134On produce of the field they fed, imbibed of the vine,
135They gorged their systems with syrupy pudding,
136They felt good from drinking the beer.
137Utterly carefree, their spirits soared,
138They ordained the destiny of Marduk their champion.
